title: Who does what to whom
can: Read sentences where someone sees, loves or has something, whatever the word order.
doneText: You can now tell the doer from the receiver by their endings, whatever order the words are in.

discover.intro: In each colour the words move around, but the meaning stays the same. Work out how Latin shows who sees whom.
discover.question: How does Latin show who sees whom?
options: The one being seen gets -m on the end: puellam, agricolam.
The first word is always the one doing the seeing.
The verb changes depending on who sees whom.
discover.nudge: Not quite. The order changes inside each colour but the meaning doesn't. Look at the word endings instead.
discover.reveal: Endings show each word's job, not word order. The doer (subject) ends in -a; the one on the receiving end (object) ends in -am. Romans usually put the verb last.

blocks.text: Each table shows one · more than one. To read a sentence: find the verb (usually last), then the doer (-a, -us, -ae, -ī), then the receiver (-am, -um, -ās, -ōs).
Spanish nouns mostly come from the Latin receiver form: rosam became rosa, mūrum became muro, amīcum became amigo, templum became templo.

blocks.title: Same words, opposite meaning
blocks.note: Only the endings swapped. The -us word does the seeing, the -um word gets seen, whatever the order.

blocks.text: Slavery was everywhere in Rome. Servī worked in houses, on farms and in mines, and many were prisoners of war. Latin texts mention them constantly, so servus is one of the first words you need.

write.title: Write it in Latin
write.task: Write three Latin sentences about a Roman farm: who sees, loves or has what. Put the verb last.
write.model: Agricola equum habet. Servus dominum videt. Puella equum amat.
checklist: The doer ends in -a or -us, the receiver in -am or -um
The verb comes last and ends in -t (one) or -nt (more than one)

boss.title: Reading: the farmer and the horse
boss.persona: You are Magistra Līvia, a warm Latin teacher. The learner knows est and sunt, nouns in -a and -us (doer and receiver forms, singular and plural), neuter -um nouns and 3rd-person verbs (videt, vident, amat, habet, laudat). Chat in English and give very short Latin sentences about a Roman farm using only these, so they can practise finding the doer and the receiver.

choices: The farmer has a horse.
The horse has a farmer.
Equum ends in -um: the horse is what the farmer has.
The farmers have a horse.
Agricola and habet are singular.
The girl loves the horse.
The horse loves the girl.
Equum (-um) is the receiver and puella (-a) the doer, whatever the order.
The girl loves the horses.
Equum is one horse. Horses would be equōs.
The slaves see the temple and praise it.
The slave sees the temple and praises it.
Servī and the -nt verbs are plural: slaves.
The temple sees the slaves and praises them.
Servī (-ī) is the plural doer, and the -nt verbs agree with it.
The master does not praise the slaves.
The slaves do not praise the master.
Dominus (-us) is the doer, servōs (-ōs) the receivers.
The master praises the slaves.
Nōn means not.
